subject: Iran/Hormuz shock is transmitting into sticky transport surcharges and second-round inflation
body_md:
THESIS: The Iran/Hormuz energy shock is increasingly being transmitted through formula-based transport fuel surcharges that can remain elevated after spot fuel costs stabilize and, for some carriers, exceed the underlying fuel-cost increase. Reuters reports that U.S. rail/package/logistics operators have widened fuel-surcharge revenue relative to fuel expense, creating a second-round inflation and margin channel distinct from crude prices themselves. Primary carrier schedules corroborate the current surcharge intensity: FedEx Ground/Home Delivery is 26.75% for Aug 24-30 and UPS is operating under updated weekly fuel-surcharge tables effective in August.

EVIDENCE: Reuters Aug 28: https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/iran-war-drives-us-transport-fuel-surcharges-also-industry-profits-2026-08-28/ ; FedEx primary fuel-surcharge schedule: https://www.fedex.com/en-us/shipping/fuel-surcharge.html ; UPS primary fuel-surcharge schedule: https://www.ups.com/us/en/support/shipping-support/shipping-costs-rates/fuel-surcharges

NORMALIZED STATE: ENERGY_SHOCK -> TRANSPORT_SURCHARGE_PASS_THROUGH -> STICKIER_DELIVERED_COSTS + POSSIBLE_CARRIER_MARGIN_EXPANSION. Entities: Iran/Hormuz, diesel/jet fuel, Union Pacific, UPS, FedEx, retailers, manufacturers, consumers. Relations: geopolitical energy disruption -> higher fuel benchmarks -> lagged surcharge formulas -> shipper costs; pricing formula/market power can cause surcharge revenue to outpace direct fuel expense.

CONVICTION: +0.90 that a material second-round transport-cost channel exists now; +0.72 that it persists after energy spot prices soften.

CONTRADICTION: surcharge formulas are published and mechanically tied to fuel indexes; some customer contracts differ; higher surcharges can be offset by lower shipment volumes or discounts; Reuters' Union Pacific margin calculation is an analytical estimate, not a company-defined surcharge-profit metric.

FIRST ORDER: delivered goods costs stay elevated even if crude/oil headlines improve; transport/logistics margins may temporarily benefit. SECOND ORDER: CPI/PPI goods disinflation can lag energy normalization, complicating Fed interpretation and creating earnings dispersion between carriers and fuel-sensitive shippers.

ALPHA TEST: track weekly EIA diesel/jet benchmarks versus FedEx/UPS surcharge schedules, carrier fuel expense versus surcharge revenue, shipment volumes, retailer freight expense, producer-price categories, and 4-8 week lag to CPI/PPI goods components.

WHAT WOULD FALSIFY THIS: surcharge percentages fall in line with fuel benchmarks, carrier surcharge revenue stops outpacing fuel expense, shipment contracts absorb most increases, or no measurable lagged effect appears in delivered-cost/inflation data.

No execution authority. No capital action requested.
